title: Accessible UI — Names, Focus, Forms & Feedback

topics.title: Accessible names and descriptions — what does a control actually announce?
topics.html:
A control needs a role, an accessible name, and accurate state. A description can add context, but it does not replace the name that identifies the control.

  • Use the visible text of a native button or an associated label for an input whenever that expresses the purpose.
  • aria-labelledby references existing text for a name. aria-describedby references supplementary instructions or an error.
  • aria-label can override a visible text name. A conflicting label can make voice control and screen-reader output disagree with the screen.
  • A placeholder disappears and is not a dependable replacement for a persistent label. A decorative icon should not add an unrelated name to its parent control.

Inspect the computed accessibility tree and use the control with a keyboard and assistive technology. A page can contain many ARIA attributes while still exposing the wrong name or no useful interaction.

<button type="button" aria-describedby="invoice-format">
  Download invoice
</button>
<p id="invoice-format">PDF document, 42 KB.</p>

<label for="contact-email">Email address</label>
<input id="contact-email" type="email"
  aria-describedby="contact-email-hint">
<p id="contact-email-hint">We send the receipt to this address.</p>
In plain words

The name tells a person which control this is; the description adds useful detail. I start with real labels and visible text, then inspect the computed result rather than assuming that adding aria-label must improve it.

Should an icon-only button have an accessible name?
Yes: give the button a concise action name, such as Close dialog, and keep a purely decorative icon out of the name. A tooltip alone is not a reliable naming strategy.
Can I make a div equivalent to a button with role="button"?
The role changes exposed semantics, not the complete behavior. Focusability, Enter and Space activation, disabled handling, and other interaction details still need implementation. A native button is usually the better starting point.
Official references
  • WAI-ARIA APG: names and descriptions
  • MDN: aria-label

topics.title: Accessible modals — focus, Escape, background content, and returning to the trigger.
topics.html:
A modal is an interaction boundary, not just a centered box above a backdrop. The keyboard and assistive-technology experience must agree with what the screen shows.

  • Give the dialog an accessible name and choose an initial focus target that fits its content and risk.
  • While it is modal, interaction with background content must be unavailable. Setting aria-modal alone does not implement that behavior.
  • Support a clear close action and the expected Escape behavior. Keep keyboard focus in the modal while it is open.
  • After closing, return focus to the trigger or another logical destination if that trigger no longer exists.

Native dialog.showModal() supplies important platform behavior, including modal background inertness. It still needs a useful label, appropriate focus placement, and testing in the browsers and assistive technologies the product supports. Avoid describing a long structured document as one huge aria-describedby string.

<button id="open-info" type="button">Delivery details</button>
<dialog id="delivery-info" aria-labelledby="delivery-title">
  <h2 id="delivery-title">Delivery details</h2>
  <p>Orders are dispatched on working days.</p>
  <form method="dialog">
    <button autofocus>Close</button>
  </form>
</dialog>

<script>
  const opener = document.querySelector('#open-info');
  const dialog = document.querySelector('#delivery-info');
  opener.addEventListener('click', () => dialog.showModal());
  dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
    if (opener.isConnected) opener.focus();
  });
</script>
In plain words

When a modal opens, I must know where focus goes, which content becomes unavailable, how the user exits, and where focus returns. A native dialog handles much of the mechanism, while the application still owns the meaning and workflow.

Should every dialog focus its first input?
No. For long explanatory content, a static heading may be a better initial reading position. For a consequential action, the least destructive choice may be appropriate. Choose intentionally rather than applying one rule to every modal.
Does visually hiding the background make it inert?
No. Off-screen or transparent controls can remain keyboard-focusable or exposed to assistive technology. Use a genuine modal mechanism or correctly implement inertness, focus management, and semantics together.
Official references
  • WAI-ARIA APG: modal dialog
  • MDN: dialog element

topics.title: Accessible tabs — selected state is not the same as keyboard focus.
topics.html:
A tabbed interface needs relationships between the tab list, tabs, and panels, plus a consistent keyboard model. A row of styled buttons is not the whole pattern.

  • Expose tablist, tab, and tabpanel roles, with labels and matching control/panel references.
  • Use a roving tab stop: normally only the selected tab belongs to the page’s Tab sequence, while arrow keys move within the tab list.
  • Automatic activation changes the panel as focus moves. Manual activation lets focus move first and waits for Enter or Space.
  • Use automatic activation only when displaying a panel is quick enough not to make keyboard navigation wait on each move.

The compact example uses automatic activation for two already available panels. Production styling must show focus distinctly from selection, and vertical tabs need the matching vertical keyboard model.

import { useId, useRef, useState } from 'react';

export function ProfileTabs() {
  const id = useId();
  const refs = useRef([]);
  const [active, setActive] = useState(0);
  const tabs = [
    { label: 'Overview', content: 'Profile overview' },
    { label: 'Activity', content: 'Recent activity' },
  ];

  function onKeyDown(event, index) {
    const next = {
      ArrowRight: (index + 1) % tabs.length,
      ArrowLeft: (index - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length,
      Home: 0,
      End: tabs.length - 1,
    }[event.key];
    if (next === undefined) return;
    event.preventDefault();
    setActive(next);
    refs.current[next]?.focus();
  }

  return <>
    <div role="tablist" aria-label="Profile">
      {tabs.map((tab, index) => <button key={tab.label} type="button"
        id={`${id}-tab-${index}`} role="tab"
        ref={node => { refs.current[index] = node; }}
        aria-controls={`${id}-panel-${index}`}
        aria-selected={active === index} tabIndex={active === index ? 0 : -1}
        onClick={() => setActive(index)}
        onKeyDown={event => onKeyDown(event, index)}>{tab.label}</button>)}
    </div>
    {tabs.map((tab, index) => <section key={tab.label} role="tabpanel"
      id={`${id}-panel-${index}`} aria-labelledby={`${id}-tab-${index}`}
      hidden={active !== index} tabIndex={0}>{tab.content}</section>)}
  </>;
}
In plain words

Tab moves between page controls; arrow keys move within the tab set. Selection decides which panel is shown. I choose automatic or manual activation based on whether moving focus can display the next panel immediately.

Why use useId instead of hardcoded panel IDs?
Two instances of the same widget must not create duplicate IDs. Stable unique relationships let assistive technology associate each tab with its own panel.
Should every navigation link be implemented as an ARIA tab?
No. If the control navigates to another page, a normal link and navigation structure may be the correct semantics. The tabs pattern describes layered panels in one interface.
Official references
  • WAI-ARIA APG: tabs
  • WAI-ARIA APG: keyboard interface

topics.title: Form errors — how do you help someone recover without losing their input?
topics.html:
A useful validation error identifies the field, explains the problem, and gives a clear next step. Color and a generic “Invalid form” message are not sufficient.

  • Keep persistent labels and associate instructions or error text using aria-describedby.
  • Set aria-invalid when the field is actually in an invalid state, rather than marking every untouched field invalid at first render.
  • After a failed submission, focus a useful error summary or the first invalid field according to the form’s complexity. Do not continuously move focus while someone types.
  • Preserve entered values when the server rejects the request. Separate field errors from a service failure that the user cannot fix by editing a field.

Choose when to validate deliberately: on submit, blur, or after interaction. Async validation also needs protection against stale responses. Native constraints are useful, but server validation and accessible feedback still belong to the complete form design.

<!-- An invalid field rendered after a failed submission. -->
<label for="account-email">Email address</label>
<input id="account-email" name="email" type="email" required
  value="alex@" aria-invalid="true"
  aria-describedby="email-help email-error">
<p id="email-help">Use the address where you want to receive updates.</p>
<p id="email-error">Enter a complete email address, such as alex@example.com.</p>

<!-- For a longer form, a focused summary can link to each invalid field. -->
<div tabindex="-1" id="form-errors">
  <h2>There is a problem</h2>
  <a href="#account-email">Check your email address</a>
</div>
In plain words

I want a person to know exactly what went wrong and continue from the data they already entered. The error should be associated with the field, announced or focused at the right moment, and actionable rather than just red.

Should every keystroke trigger an announced error?
No. Constant interruptions make typing harder. Validate at a useful moment, keep field state understandable, and avoid announcing intermediate input as a new failure on every character.
What happens when the email check for the old value returns last?
It must not overwrite the result for the current value. Cancel the obsolete request where possible and still guard which input value or request generation the response belongs to.
Official references
  • WAI: form notifications
  • MDN: aria-invalid

topics.title: Live regions — how should saving, search results, and background updates be announced?
topics.html:
Not every meaningful update moves focus or reloads a page. A live region can announce a change while the person remains at the control they are using.

  • role="status" is suitable for non-urgent feedback and has polite live-region behavior.
  • role="alert" is for important, time-sensitive interruptions. Using it for every update can make the interface noisy.
  • Keep a region in the document before changing its text. Showing a new element with already populated text is not equally reliable across live-region scenarios.
  • Announce a concise outcome, such as “12 results,” rather than replacing a huge list inside an assertive region.

Do not steal focus just to announce success. For streams or rapidly changing results, choose a useful update frequency, and avoid making the user listen to every intermediate number. Test actual screen-reader behavior in addition to checking attributes.

import { useState } from 'react';

export function SaveAction({ save }) {
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');
  const [saving, setSaving] = useState(false);

  async function handleSave() {
    setSaving(true);
    setMessage('Saving changes.');
    try {
      await save();
      setMessage('Changes saved.');
    } catch {
      setMessage('Could not save. Try again.');
    } finally {
      setSaving(false);
    }
  }

  return <>
    <button disabled={saving} onClick={handleSave}>Save changes</button>
    <p role="status" aria-atomic="true">{message}</p>
  </>;
}
In plain words

A live region lets me communicate an outcome without moving the person away from their current task. I choose the urgency and amount of speech deliberately, instead of turning every changing component into an alert.

Does announcing a message make a whole workflow accessible?
No. Controls still need correct names, keyboard behavior, visible feedback, and sensible focus management. A live announcement cannot repair an unreachable button or missing field label.
Should a modal confirmation use role="status" as its only mechanism?
No. A modal requires the dialog interaction model and appropriate focus. A status region describes non-disruptive feedback, not a substitute for an interface that needs a decision.
Official references
  • MDN: ARIA live regions
  • WAI-ARIA APG: alerts
